spec.name: Dutch Windmill
spec.description: A chunky, pastel Animal Crossing-style Dutch windmill: a tapering octagonal cream tower on a brick plinth, a teal shingled cap, four big cloth-and-lattice sails, a tail pole with winch, and a cosy porch door with flower boxes and flour sacks.
spec.layout:
Front is +Z, up is +Y, the model is centred on x=0 and stands on y=0. It is a toy-like windmill with soft rounded shapes, thick cream trim, oversized windows and warm pastel flat colours.

OCTAGONAL TOWER (apothem = centre to flat face): the plinth is y 0..0.5 with apothem 2.5 (circumradius 2.71) in brick, with a stone course on top. The tower rises from y 0.5 to y 5.0 and tapers linearly from apothem 2.2 at y 0.5 to apothem 1.45 at y 5.0 (circumradius 2.38 to 1.57). Every octagon has flat faces at the cardinal directions and vertices at 22.5 degrees, so a flat face points at +Z. The plinth, tower, curb and cap ring all use this orientation. Face azimuths run from +Z toward +X (the model's left): 0 = front, 45 = front-left, 90 = left, 135, 180 = back, 225, 270 = right, 315 = front-right. The tower body is cream plaster with soft horizontal shade bands, brick-red corner quoins and two thin brick bands at y 2.2 and y 4.3.

DOOR AND PORCH: the front-left face (azimuth 45, outward dir [0.707,0,0.707]) holds the door at doorCenter [1.56,0.5,1.56]. A small covered porch projects to apothem 3.1 (box x/z 0.8..3.0) with a roof at y 2.5. It stays clear of the front sail, which only occupies |x|<0.6 below the hub.

CAP: it rotates on the cap joint, sits on the curb at y 5.0, and is a rounded boat/dome shape with teal shingle rows. The ridge runs front to back. Cap radius is about 1.75 at the eaves (y 5.15) and the top is about y 6.95. A snout housing at the front reaches z 2.0 and holds the sail shaft. There is a finial and a small round window, and a weather vane sits on top.

SAILS: the rotor joint is at the hub [0,5.9,2.1] with its axis along +Z. The shaft nose and hub boss run z 2.1..2.75. The sails lie in the plane z=2.45 in a rest '+' shape (arms up, down, left, right), each 4.6 m from the hub centre to its tip. Each sail has a thick wooden stock, a lattice frame about 1.1 wide from r=1.0 to r=4.6, cream cloth panels on the trailing half, and a red stripe and tip cap. The sail tip reaches y 10.5 at the top and y 1.3 at the bottom, with x +-4.6.

TAIL: a tail pole runs from the cap's back (mount capBack [0,5.5,-1.7]) sloping down to a ground stake at [0,0,-4.3]. It carries a spoked winch wheel, a ladder, and a small bunting streamer.

STYLE: everything is a simple chunky base shape, slightly oversized and softened, with small details as separate parts in their own flat colours: cream trim rings, rounded window frames, shingle rows, rivets, flower dots. No part is textured or realistic. Warm tones sit on top and cooler tones underneath. Make a window glass pane glow soft yellow with the glow kit. Only small cosy props are included (flower boxes, sacks, barrel, lantern). No ground plane.

parts.builds: The brick plinth (y 0..0.5, apothem 2.5) with a stone cap course, brick base bands, and the tapering octagonal cream plaster tower (apothem 2.2 down to 1.45, y 0.5..5.0) as faceted lathes, extrudes or lofts. It has plaster shade bands, brickDark corner quoins up all 8 vertical edges, brick bands at y 2.2 and 4.3, and a cream trim ring and brick curb at y 5.0 (apothem 1.55..1.62, top at y 5.15). Windows go on faces 90, 270, 135, 225 and 315 only; the door face 45 and the front face 0 are left plain except for a plaster patch. Each window has a chunky cream frame, sill and lintel, a glassBlue pane (glow the pane with the glow kit) and wood shutters with small heart or diamond cut-outs. There is a round window at face 315. The back face 180 gets a loft hatch with a hoisting beam, a small pulley and a rope with a hook. Add a few stone patches and brick patches on the plinth, and a little lantern on a bracket at face 270. Cosy rounded Animal Crossing look; no door on this part.
parts.attaches: Rests on the floor at ground. Its top meets the cap at mount towerTop / capCurb. The door, porch and flower boxes on face 45 belong to porchDoor, which attaches at doorCenter and porchFloor.

parts.builds: The rotating cap on the cap joint, sitting on capCurb. It has a flush cream ring on the curb and a rounded boat-shaped dome in roofTeal. Its eaves radius is about 1.75 at y 5.15 and the top is about y 6.95, with an elongated snout reaching z 2.0 at capFrontShaft and a shorter tail end at z -1.9. It has rows of shingles (small overlapping plates alternating roofTeal, roofTealLight and roofTealDark), a cream ridge beam with a gold finial ball, and a weather vane (metal arrow and gold ball) on top. The front snout has a wood face-plate with the shaft bearing hole (the shaft nose is built by sails), and a small round porthole window with a cream frame on each side. A pair of short wood brackets sits at capBack to take the tail pole. Add a bargeboard trim in trimCream along the front gable edge, and a few leaf-shaped clay accents.
parts.attaches: Sits on the tower curb (mounts towerTop, capCurb). Its front snout meets the sails shaft at capFrontShaft / hub. Its back meets the tail pole at capBack.

parts.builds: The whole rotor on the rotor joint: a wood shaft from inside the cap nose out to z 2.75, a rounded wood hub boss with a gold nose cap and rivet ring at hub / sailPlane, and four identical sails in a '+' shape (up, down, left, right) in the plane z=2.45, each 4.6 m from the hub centre to its tip. Each sail has a thick wooden stock (woodLight) along its axis, and a lattice frame about 1.1 wide from r=1.0 to r=4.6 with two woodDark side rails and cross bars every 0.4 m. Cream sailCloth panels fill the trailing half of the frame (a few panels in each lattice cell, slightly rolled at the edge) with a sailRed stripe and a red tip cap. Small gold bolts sit at the bar crossings, and each tip has a small wood finial. A little cream pennant on the top sail tip. Build each sail once with a helper and rotate it for the other three.
parts.attaches: Shaft enters the cap snout at capFrontShaft; hub at mount hub. Keep the lowest sail tip above y 1.1. It must clear the porch roof (x >= 0.8 at the porch).

parts.builds: The tail pole and its fittings, riding the cap joint. A thick woodLight beam runs from the cap back at capBack [0,5.5,-1.7] sloping down to tailStake [0,0,-4.3] with a rounded end. Two A-frame braces sit near the cap, with a wood ladder (two rails and rungs) alongside the pole's lower half. A chunky spoked winch wheel (woodDark rim, wood spokes, gold hub, metal axle) is mounted on two posts at about 1/3 up the pole. A fat rope (cream, a few coil segments) is wound on the winch. A wood ground stake at tailStake carries a metal ring and ground rope loops and has a small stone footing, plus a red-and-cream bunting streamer of 5 small flags hanging between the pole and the cap. Small leafy sprigs at the stake base in leaf green.
parts.attaches: Top ends at capBack on the cap joint. The foot stake rests on the floor at tailStake.

parts.builds: Everything on tower face 45 (outward dir [0.707,0,0.707]) plus the cosy props. The door on joint doorHinge is a rounded-arch wood door in doorBlue with woodDark plank lines, a gold knob, strap hinges and a small round window. It has a thick cream frame with an arch, a keystone and a nameplate. The porch is a small covered stoop projecting to apothem 3.1 (centre porchFloor [2.19,0.5,2.19]) with a stone slab floor, two chunky wood posts with brackets, a lean-to roof of roofTeal shingle rows at y 2.5 (porchRoof) with a cream fascia, and two stone steps down to the ground. Above the door sits a round glowing glowYellow window with a cream frame. Props: two window flower boxes (wood, pink and yellow flowers, leaf green) on the porch rails, two sacks of flour (sack, tied necks, small ink-coloured label marks) and one wood barrel with metal hoops beside the steps, a hanging lantern (metal frame, glowYellow glass, glowing) under the porch roof, and a small welcome mat. Keep every prop chunky and rounded.
parts.attaches: Backs on tower face 45 at doorCenter and plinthTop, with the door hinging at doorHinge. The porch floor starts at y 0.5 on the plinth, steps reach y 0. The porch roof stays below the sail plane region (sails only occupy |x|<0.6 below y 5).

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching the structure for a Dutch windmill in Animal Crossing style, planning a joint hierarchy with a root base, a cap, and a rotating hub for the sails so they can spin.

Now I'm working through realistic yet stylized proportions: an octagonal tapering tower around 5-6m tall, a boat-shaped cap roughly 1.2m high, and sails spanning about 9m across mounted on a hub near the top, making sure the lowest sail tip clears the ground via a small gallery stage. I'm calculating overall bounding dimensions—height near 10.7m and width near 9.4m—accounting for the sail arms' reach beyond the tower itself.

I'm settling on a soft Animal Crossing-inspired palette: cream plaster walls, a red-orange brick plinth, and warm terracotta tones for the cap, keeping everything rounded and pastel rather than harshly realistic.

Now I'm working out the windmill's sail geometry — positioning the hub and shaft forward from the tapered cap, figuring out the sail plane's offset so it clears the tower radius at ground level, and sizing the sail arms to extend well above and below the hub for a balanced silhouette.

I realize the gallery platform would collide with the lowest sail tip, so I'm skipping the stage structure and reconsidering door placement — since the sails sweep in front at z 2.35, I need to offset the door off-center rather than dead-center on the front face to avoid it being blocked by the rotating arm.

I'll place the door on the face at 45° toward +X with a small porch step and window above, plus a side balcony, and add a simple stone ring base with a round step. Now I'm breaking the mill into five parts, starting with the tower base — tapered octagon walls, brick bands, corner trim, plaster, door, windows, steps, dentils, and lanterns, sized as a box roughly 5.4 units wide and 5 tall with a budget of 190 — followed by the cap with a ring curb and a rounded terracotta dome.

Now I'm detailing the remaining pieces: the sails rotor with a hub boss, shaft, four lattice-framed sails with cloth and spars, and the tail and gallery assembly, including the fantail wheel and tail pole with winch and ladder descending to ground level.

I'll add a round stone path pad and a small signboard near the entrance, keeping props modest for that Animal Crossing charm. The door, porch, steps, shutters, flower boxes, sacks, and barrel belong to part 5 "doorway," positioned where the door face meets the tower, while sail blades extend horizontally near the top separate from this cluster.

Actually, I realize placing the door on a cardinal face near the sails risks collision, so instead I'll put the door on a 45° diagonal face of the octagonal tower, away from the rotating sail plane. I'm working out the apothem radius at ground level tapering upward to position the door opening correctly on that angled face.

Now I'm working out the tower's geometry in detail: the door mount position and orientation, the plinth's apothem and circumradius from 0 to 0.5, the tapering tower body from 0.5 to 5.0, and the cap curb, overhang ring, and dome proportions up to the top at 7.0, including where the hub element should sit near the cap front.

I'm also figuring out the rotor joint placement, sail arm lengths and their extent above and below hub height, overall bounding box dimensions accounting for the symmetric sails and front porch, and the tail pole's position and length running from the cap back down and outward.

For the floor and joint rig, I'm marking the tail pole's foot as the floor-touching point while leaving the sails and rotor exempt. Then I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: mill as root spine, cap as hinge child of mill, and rotor as a hinge child of cap grouped with the sails—plus considering a door hinge joint off mill for the door builder to use.

Now I'm working out the door hinge's exact position, placing it along the tangent of the tower face at 45 degrees offset from the door center, and reconciling how the door sits flush against the plinth top where the plinth's wider apothem meets the tower face.

I'm then positioning the porch so it extends outward from the plinth at a larger apothem, checking its corner coordinates against the tower's footprint to confirm the width and placement stay within reasonable bounds on both sides.

Now I'm settling on a color palette capped at 24 swatches, picking out cream and shaded plaster tones, brick reds, stone grays, and switching the roof to a teal-green shingle look with a lighter accent, plus trim whites and wood tones for structural details.

Rounding out the palette with sail cloth and frame colors, striped red sail accents, glowing window glass, ink outlines, floral pinks and yellows, leaf green, metal gray, and gold accents—landing right around 24 total. Then I'm breaking the model into five main parts: the tower body with its bands and multi-level windows, the cap, the rotor, the tail and fan assembly, and the porch.

Checking the triangle budget across parts—180, 170, 230, 120, 160—comes to 860, safely under the 900 cap, with the door attached to the porch via a hinge joint. I'm also noting the overall style: rounded and chunky with soft pastels, thick trim, oversized windows, flat colors, and small leaf/flower motifs suggesting stitched cloth. Now I need to write precise layout instructions so builders stay aligned—specifying the tower's apothem formula, confirming the octagon orientation with flat faces toward cardinal directions and vertices at 22.5°, and detailing the cap geometry including curb height and dome profile radius.

I'm working out the cap's full shape rising to a top height of 6.9, extended forward into a snout for the shaft housing, with a front gable and ridge along the z-axis, plus mount points for the hub, tower top, cap back, door center, and front shaft. For the sails, I'm detailing each arm's wooden spar length and radius, the lattice frame with rails and cross bars, and cream cloth panels with red stripe pennants at the tips, along with precise width and radius dimensions for the sail frame.

Now I'm placing the sail plane position and hub boss, then moving to the tail assembly: a tail pole running from the cap back down to a ground stake, with a spoked winch wheel, ladder rungs, cross braces, a stake post with ring, a sagging rope, and maybe a small lantern and flag at the end, all within a budgeted part count for the tail section.

I'm then working out which bounding box each part occupies so the tower, porch, and tail pieces don't overlap incorrectly, deciding that the porch owns the door, frame, surround, and window above the door, while the tower owns side windows placed away from the front sail shaft so they aren't obstructed by it.

I'm naming faces by azimuth angle and assigning windows at the left/right (90/270), front-right (315), and diagonal (135/225) positions at varying heights, plus a back hatch door at the top with a hoisting beam for loft access. Now I'm ready to write the final JSON with descriptions that are thorough but concise.

I'm planning the buildSails function, placing the rotor joint at the hub with a +Z axis and positioning the sail geometry using the rotor bone, with the sail plane set at z=2.45.

I'm working out a helper to place each sail at an angle around the hub: computing direction and perpendicular vectors from theta, then figuring the right rotation offset so the box's local Y axis aligns with the arm direction, and deriving a position function combining the hub location with radial and lateral offsets plus vertical height above the sail plane.

Now I'm sizing the sail components for each arm, starting with the main stock box—its width, thickness, and length spanning from near the hub out to the tip, checking that the extreme positions stay within reasonable bounds relative to the hub height.

Then I'm adding side rails flanking the stock, end bars at both extremes, and cross bars spaced evenly along the frame to give the sail its lattice structure.

Bolts would balloon the part count if placed individually at every crossing, so I'll merge them into one geometry per sail to stay within budget—roughly 55 parts allotted per sail across stock, rails, bars, cloth, bolts, and trim.

Since bolts are spheres and rotationally symmetric, I can just compute their positions directly in model space and translate, skipping rotation matrices entirely. Now I need to figure out which side of the stock counts as the trailing half for cloth placement, using the local x-axis orientation relative to the arm angle.

For the cloth panels, I'm placing nine small box panels in the lattice cells, sized to fit within each cell's gap and positioned just behind the bars. I'm also considering adding a small cylinder along each panel's lower edge to suggest a slightly rolled fabric edge.

I'll switch to quaternion-based rotation for tilting the cloth, combining a yaw and tilt quaternion for the sail twist. For the red accents, I'm planning a longitudinal stripe near v=0.3 with a narrow width, plus a separate red tip cap.

Adding the tip cap and lattice cross bars...

Still working out panel placement...

Tallying parts: with 16 louvre panels per sail and the other components, I land around 140 for the sails, plus hub and pennant pieces, keeping the total safely under 230 with simple box geometry. I'm also considering adding a thin lengthwise lattice rod on the leading half of each arm for extra detail.

Now I'm working out cloth panel placement on the trailing half of each sail—centering subpanels with a gap between them, applying consistent tilt for a corrugated look, and setting up the hub shaft as a cylinder running along the central axis.

For the hub itself, I'm sketching it as a layered construction: a back flange cylinder in dark wood, then a main drum section in regular wood, building out the boss shape from stacked cylindrical segments rather than a single complex form.

I'm placing the rivets on the flange rim instead, since the drum covers the inner radius—putting eight small gold spheres at radius 0.46, z 2.28 around the visible flange band. Then I need to check the stocks crossing through the hub at the sail plane, since that depth range overlaps the drum's z-span.

Since both stock bars share the same depth and only overlap inside the drum, that's fine to leave coplanar. I'm also adding a metal band ring around the drum at r 0.44, z 2.4 with slight thickness, letting the stocks pass through it since they're on different surfaces and won't z-fight.

I'll offset the pennant flag to extend from the mast toward -x, giving it a swallowtail shape with a small red stripe accent, and add a slight wave to its outline for a fluttering effect.

For the arm tips, I'm placing small cone-shaped wood finials pointing outward, sized and rotated so their axis aligns with the arm direction, checking that the lowest tip still clears the required height.

Now I'm setting up helper functions to build sail parts using position and rotation data, computing local coordinates for each sail based on angle, direction vectors, and offsets to place points correctly in 3D space.

I'm also planning the color palette, giving wood, sail cloth, gold, and trim distinct tones, and considering alternating sailCloth and plaster shades across panels for visual texture.

For the sail arms, I'm setting angles at 90, 270, 0, and 180 degrees for the plus shape, and adding a rolled trim cylinder along each arm positioned near the edge of the panel with a slight vertical lift, using the trimCream color for the rail detail.

Placing a red stripe to bridge the narrow gap between subpanels, then adding gold bolt spheres along the bars at front-facing positions calculated from the stock depth.

I'm merging 27 bolt spheres into a single geometry for efficiency, attaching it to the rotor bone, and adding a thin dark-wood rod along the leading edge for lattice slats, skipping diagonal bracing for now before moving on to writing the hub position code.

Now I'm constructing the hub itself from cylinders oriented along the Z axis: a central shaft spanning the hub's length, a ring of small rivet spheres embedded at the flange's front face, and the flange cylinder sized to fit around them.

Positioning the claw at radius 0.75 with length 0.5 so it sits between drum and lattice without overlap, and adding two bolts into it at radii 0.65 and 0.85. Then I'm setting up the pennant extrusion with its outline, thickness, and bone attachment, plus starting the mast as a thin box.

Adding the red stripe detail to the flag geometry, then finalizing the finial and pennant positioning before writing the actual mesh-building code with the necessary imports.

I'll keep the Ctx type as given in the function signature without importing it, since types erase at runtime anyway. For the tail pole geometry, I'm planning it to run from the back cap position down to a lower point behind.

Now I'm working out the exact coordinates — aiming the pole's rounded bottom end to sit near ground level, around y 0.2-0.3, with a slight radius so it doesn't clip below the floor, and considering adding a separate stake post near the pole's base to anchor it.

I'll use the rod helper for straight members with faceted low-poly sides (8 sides, smooth off) and set up the pole as a capsule between its two endpoints.

Working out the pole's geometry now: computing its start point, direction vector, and perpendicular normals so I can orient the top surface correctly since the pole slopes down and back.

I'll place the ladder lashed alongside the pole offset toward the back face, with rails parallel to the pole axis and rungs running crosswise, spanning the lower-to-mid section. Then I still need to position the winch posts roughly a third of the way up the pole.

I realize the wheel would collide with the pole at that radius, so I'm repositioning it to the side instead, with the axle running between two posts mounted on a cross-beam bracket at t=0.58, keeping everything offset from the pole's centerline.

Working out the wheel placement in the YZ-plane with the pole position at t=0.58, computing the center coordinates and radius bounds, then figuring out the support posts connecting the pole bracket points to the axle center.

Now I'm designing the wheel rim as a torus oriented along the x-axis with spokes radiating out to it from the center.

Next I'm adding a gold hub cylinder at the center, handle pegs sticking out at the spoke tips like capstan handles, and a wooden rope drum mounted on the axle to hold the coiled cream rope.

Checking clearance so the rope path from the drum to the stake ring stays just outside the pole radius along its length, interpolating z-position at each y value to confirm it doesn't clip the pole's surface.

I'm checking the ring's placement on the stake and noticing the stake and pole positions nearly overlap at the bottom — I need to nudge the stake further out to avoid the collision.

Skipping full rope lashing for simplicity, I'll add a small ring loop on the stake's side, positioning its torus so it just touches the stake's edge, plus a small eye bolt detail nearby.

For the rope, I'm adding flat coiled loops lying on the ground near the stake with a connecting curve from the ring down to them, then a stone footing cylinder at the pole's base and a few small rock shapes scattered around it.

I'm picking out the overall color palette for stone, wood, metal, sail cloth, and foliage tones, plus adding a couple A-frame braces near the top of the pole angling out to support the cap structure.

I'm working out where each A-frame brace's feet should attach along the cap's curved rim, checking whether the foot coordinates land inside or outside the dome radius at that height.

Adding iron collar details at the apexes, gold bolts at the feet, and banded rings around the pole with slight taper. I'm also throwing in a pivot block and planning small bunting flags strung between the pole and cap.

Placing flags along a sagging quadratic bezier curve between the cap and pole, alternating red and cream colors across five triangular flags, with a thin rope swept along the same curve connecting them.

I'm recalculating the string endpoints and sag between the cap and pole to avoid clashing with the A-frame legs, trying a few alternate anchor points on the right side so the bunting and flags sit clear of the structure.

I'm worried the leg line and bunting string might cross visually, so I'm adjusting the A-frame positions slightly and repositioning the bunting to run from lower on the pole out to the cap point, accepting a small overlap as fine.

Checking the bunting length and sag, I'll keep five flags hanging vertically, evenly spaced along the swag. But I realize the hook position at x=1.3 pokes outside the box bounds, so I need to pull it inward to around x=0.75-0.78, placing it right at the cap eave where the curb radius keeps it visible rather than buried inside the shell.

Now I'm adding leafy sprigs around the stake base using small angled cones for leaves plus sphere clumps for fullness, with five sprigs arranged around the base point using randomized variation for a natural look. For the ladder, I'm positioning the rails offset from the pole axis by the pole radius plus a small gap, running them along the top normal direction.

Widening the ladder to x ±0.27 with rail and rung radii set, spacing rungs roughly every 0.28 units along the pole, and checking the rail endpoints clear the floor properly.

Adjusting the pole offset to 0.16 so the ladder rails sit flush against the tapered pole surface without gaps, and verifying the rungs don't collide with the pole's inner radius at that distance. Now I'm setting up a small rod helper function to draw cylindrical connectors between points for the ladder structure.

Checking the capsule's round end cap doesn't poke through the pole's top bounds, then working out the vector math for the pole's direction and a perpendicular vector in the YZ plane to orient things correctly.

Writing box placement logic...

I'll simplify to just a few metal and dark wood bands near the stake ends instead of fussing over stripes. For the stake itself, I'm giving it a rounded top, sinking the base flush with the ground, and adding small cream rope loops as tori wrapped around it at a few heights, plus flat loops lying near the base on the ground.

I'm checking placement carefully so the ground loops don't clip into the stone footing -- shifting their position and radius so they clear the footing's extent, then planning a connecting rope curve running from the ring to the loop.

Now I need two rope segments: one from the drum wrapping to the stake's loops near the top, and another from the ring down to the ground loops. I'm figuring out the start point for the drum rope, offset from the drum's center.

Checking the rope curve clears the pole at multiple heights and ends properly looped around the stake, staying within radius constraints. Verifying overall structure heights stay within bounds, then moving to define the wheel rim torus geometry with its center, axis, and radius.

Adding wheel details, spokes, hub...

Positioning posts clear of the wheel radius, then adding rim pegs as small cylinders and checking the drum/rope placement doesn't clip the posts.

Still refining the drum and torus placement, aligning the rope start with the drum coils. I'm sketching helper functions for generating rods and part geometry, including options for thinner sides on small components.

Placing sprigs...

Checking footing placement...

Now I'm positioning sprigs around the stake, worried the ring radius pushes slightly outside the box at z=-4.5, so I'll tighten the radius and limit sprigs to angles facing front/sides rather than all around to avoid overflow.

I'm attaching the ring to the stake with a short connecting rod, adding a small metal collar torus on the stake, then working out the bunting string geometry—defining a bezier path from a hook point near the cap eave to a control point to a point on the pole, with a small metal ball marking the hook attachment.

Adding flag trim triangles...

Setting the specific foot and apex coordinates for both A-frames to vary their height and spread slightly, then moving to the ladder setup... Placing the rails and rungs along the pole...

Now I'm defining helper functions for positioning points relative to the pole axis, then building out the winch structure: brackets, an axle, support posts, and diagonal braces, all with specific coordinates and wood materials for a sturdier mechanical look.

Then I'm adding two rim tori offset slightly along X to give the wheel some thickness, checking that the spoke length and wheel radius keep everything positioned correctly relative to the ground. I'm verifying clearances — making sure the wheel doesn't clip the ladder or the rope hanging from the drum, checking the top and bottom y-extents against the pole and rope positions.

Now I'm defining the rope as a bezier curve running from the drum down to near the ground, choosing a cream/bone color to match the sack material, and setting up a sweep along that path with a small radius to give the rope its coiled form.

Then I'm adding the ground rope as a catmull-rom curve connecting the ring bottom to looped sections near the base, swept thin at radius .025, plus a couple of tori lying flat for the loops themselves, oriented so their axis points along world y. I'm also planning stake loops as tori wrapped around a vertical stake.

For the stake top I'm placing a small sphere cap, then building a footing with a cylinder base and scattering a few darker stone icosahedra around its perimeter at offset angles, flattened vertically and positioned to stay within the ground boundary.

Now I'm adding metal bands as torus rings around the pole at a few key heights, plus small gold bolt spheres on two of the bands, and finally placing a dark wooden pivot block at the top with gold bolts on its sides.

Setting up imports for randomness and curve helpers...

I'm thinking through how to type the Ctx parameter for the towerBody function without conflicting with a possibly globally-provided Ctx type, deciding to avoid redeclaring it and instead use it inline safely.

For the geometry, I'm weighing a lathe-based octagon versus a rotated CylinderGeometry with 8 segments — rotating 22.5° about Y so a flat face faces each cardinal direction, keeping shading smooth above that segment threshold.

I'm planning a helper function that builds octagonal frusta from apothem values at bottom/top, driving the tower's tapering profile with a formula and layering slightly oversized thin frusta as plaster shade bands at specific height ranges for a soft horizontal shading effect.

Now I'm figuring out corner quoins as stacked alternating-width blocks placed at each of the eight vertical edges, tapering with the tower radius and rotated to face each corner's azimuth.
